20119-ambrotox-and-limping-dick:
Ambrotox and Limping Dick is a novel that opens in a fine English garden at noon. Amaryllis Caldegard sits under a cedar tree on Bellamy's south lawn. A piece of needlework and three fresh novels lie on her table. Yet for a full hour she has neither sewn nor read a line.

That still, warm scene hints at a mind fixed on other things. Love, secrets, and country house life drive tales of this kind. The odd title pairs a strange name with a limping Dick. Readers get a period romance where calm lawns hide sharp turns ahead.
20323-that-stick:
Charlotte M. Yonge wrote That Stick, a novel of a quiet country town. Two dignified elderly ladies in black silk walk a calm street. A man of about forty hurries up to speak with them. His usually pale cheeks are flushed, and he comes breathlessly toward them.

He has the air of a managing clerk with urgent business. Yonge, a famed Victorian novelist, finds drama in such small encounters. Church, family, and duty shape the lives behind that hurried talk. Readers get Yonge's keen eye for manners, conscience, and quiet English life.
20788-storm-over-warlock:
Shann Lantee watches a Throg attack burn below his shelf of rock in Storm over Warlock. Hearing of Throg cruelty is one thing, Andre Norton writes, and seeing it is quite another. Shann shakes in his Survey Corps uniform, pinned by more than mere care.

Norton strands a young scout on a wild world where witches hold real power. Beasts, alien foes, and strange gifts test him at each turn. Her tales of lone youths on far worlds won a vast, loyal readership. This book shows her gift for brisk plots, lean prose, and worlds that feel lived in.
20837-peggy-in-her-blue-frock:
Alice shows her dimples as she takes books from the lowest shelf at home. Two years younger than Peggy, she fears the stepladder and keeps low. Eliza Orne White sets the sisters side by side in Peggy in Her Blue Frock.

White wrote warm tales of New England family life for children. Peggy, large for her age, leads with spirit while Alice follows sweetly. Small deeds, school days, and home joys fill the gentle plot. The book shows White's gift for making plain days feel rich, a gift that won her a loyal place in children's reading.
21575-poor-jack:
Tom Saunders, called Poor Jack, dates his birth to 1786 in Captain Marryat's Poor Jack of 1840. His father ties the year to the Druids being turned over to the Melpomene. Jack checks the tale and finds that event fell in January 1787.

Greenwich and the Thames banks form the book's world, as in Jacob Faithful. Many landmarks Marryat names still stand, though their uses have changed. Jack's rise from river boy to pilot is told with warmth and close detail. The book, Marryat's sixteenth, stays a loved and lasting portrait of old watermen's London and its river folk.
21756-philosopher-jack:
Jack, called Philosopher by his college friends, is nineteen and full of hard questions as this Ballantyne tale opens. His closest friend gives advice in just two words: Do, or Don't. Jack, whose other name is Edwin, argues with everyone, himself most of all. Sitting at his desk, he asks in bitterness why he was ever born.

Ballantyne takes this restless student out of his room and into a life that tests his thinking. Talk must give way to action, and fine ideas must survive rough seas and hard work. The tale mixes college humor with the author's steady moral hand. Jack's search for a reason to live gives the adventure its weight.
21854-the-woman-in-black:
A financier's murder starts this detective novel by E. C. Bentley, published in 1913 and dedicated to G. K. Chesterton. Sigsbee Manderson's scheming brain is scattered by a shot from an unknown hand. Bentley's dedication letter jokes that his only noble motive was Chesterton's pleasure, and that he owed him a book for The Man Who Was Thursday. Hamlet's words on purposes mistook head the tale.

The Woman in Black is better known in crime history as Trent's Last Case, the tale of painter-detective Philip Trent. Bentley reshaped the detective story by letting his hero reason brilliantly toward a wrong answer. The book became a landmark of the genre. Elegant, ironic, and humane, it still anchors lists of the great detective novels.
21942-dickory-dock:
A baby, a mongrel dog, and two children make the household of L. T. Meade's Dickory Dock, published about 1890. The baby is small and not particularly fair, but it has round limbs, a dimple, and a soft, half-pathetic look in its blue eyes. Its mother died at its birth, and the orphan was carried to an uncle's house. A nurse washes and feeds it in the background, but the children and the dog are its true caretakers.

They call up its smiles and keep its small world warm. Meade, author of A World of Girls, writes childhood with a practiced, tender hand. Mrs. Franklin, tall and fretful, speaks for the grown world's worries. The tale is gentle Victorian domestic fiction built around one helpless child.
22109-the-black-wolf-pack: The Black Wolf Pack is a boys' adventure novel told in the first person by a young narrator. He opens by skipping school errands at speed: a roadster, a pile of library books, and a list of jobs from Mrs. Crawford. Home and downtown pull him in two directions at once. The everyday bustle soon gives way to the outdoor mystery promised by the title.
23049-old-jack:
An old sailor tells his life in Old Jack. The narrator took an early opportunity of making Old Jack's acquaintance, for such, he says, was the name by which the man was best known. Without reluctance Jack gave his history. It is now presented to the public with certain corrections, with which younger readers, the editor trusts, will find no fault.

Sea stories told by veterans filled the magazines this tale came from. Jack's career runs through the age of sail, its storms, ports, and shipmates rendered in yarn-spinning form. The editor's light hand keeps the salt in the speech. Such pieces taught landsmen the sea's vocabulary and its hard code of luck. Old Jack himself, weathered and willing, carries the whole cargo.
23115-the-billow-and-the-rock:
Scotland's union divides opinion in The Billow and the Rock. The Union was still new when the tale opens. Scotland's wisest heads saw safety only under a king and parliament shared with England. Many great men disagreed, preferring no rule over themselves and unchecked power over their dependents.

Against that politics of lairds and loyalty, the story sets its billow and its rock, the sea's force and the faith that withstands it. Scottish tales of the Union years mixed covenant, clan, and coast in just this way. The opening argument is unusually direct, a small history lesson before the drama. Readers get both, the politics of 1707 and a tale built to make them felt.
23272-the-story-of-the-rock:
The Story of the Rock tells how a famous lighthouse was built. Its builders used one plain fact: stone outweighs timber, so a stone tower carries the weight that wind and water demand. That added weight steadied the tower against wind and water.

The plan worked. The lighthouse was not only a success at the time, it has lasted well over two centuries. Ever since its completion, it has been a highly regarded model of lighthouse building. Readers get an engineering story in plain terms: one smart choice about materials, tested by two hundred years of storms.
528-joe-the-hotel-boy-or-winning-out-by-:
Horatio Alger Jr. follows Joe, a country lad raised by a hermit, in this success tale. After a storm and a ruined home, Joe seeks a blue box, works in a summer hotel, then in a city hotel, facing swindles, mining shares, and a hotel fire. A satchel, a tree, and two evil-doers mark his road.

Alger writes in his plain moral style, praising pluck, honesty, and kind deeds. Joe wins not by luck alone but by standing firm when others cheat. Young readers will find a brisk, hopeful story of a boy who earns his place, step by step, from storm to city.
588-master-humphrey-s-clock:
Charles Dickens frames tales and sketches round an old clock keeper in this volume, first issued as a weekly miscellany. Master Humphrey, who loves his clock's voice, invites readers to gather as friends while the clock counts hours and cheats them of heaviness. A dedication to poet Samuel Rogers fronts the book.

Dickens writes in warm, bustling prose, mixing humor, pathos, and London scenes. The clock device later gave way to full novels, but these opening pieces show Dickens finding his voice. The book charms as a glimpse of a young master learning to hold a crowd week by week.
865-passing-of-the-third-floor-back:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote this tale of a Bloomsbury lodging house, where tenants live side by side in suspicion and spite. One November afternoon, a stranger takes the third-floor back room, a modest man whose quiet kindness slowly alters the house. Each lodger, from the landlady down, finds a hidden good stirred to life.

Jerome tells the story with gentle humour and a moral touch, without preaching it flat. The stranger passes through, and the house is changed by his passing. The tale, first published in 1908, has lasted as a favourite fable of kindness, and as a showcase for Jerome's warm, humane comedy.
a-selection-from-the-lyrical-poems-of-ro:
Robert Herrick's lyrical poems are gathered here in a selection arranged by Francis Turner Palgrave, who also wrote the introduction. The preface gives Herrick's dates, born 1591 and died 1674, and admits that choosing from so many fine pieces invites argument. Herrick was a country parson who wrote like a man in love with the world.

The poems praise Corinna's going a-Maying, daffodils, cherries, country fairs, and brief youth, and the famous counsel to gather rosebuds while time allows. Others turn graver, on death, prayer, and parting. Short, musical, and clear, the lyrics mix pagan delight in the senses with Christian faith, a blend that keeps Herrick read after three centuries.
arrian-anabasis-alexander-chinnock:
Arrian wrote the Anabasis of Alexander around 150 CE, drawing on eyewitness sources. E. J. Chinnock's 1884 translation presents the fullest surviving account of the conquest. Alexander's expedition opened the wonders of the East to the West.

Seven books trail the Macedonian army from Greece to India. Battles, sieges, river crossings, and mutinies unfold in campaign order. Arrian, himself a general and governor, judges Alexander's generalship professionally. He used Ptolemy and Aristobulus, officers who marched with Alexander, as sources. Chinnock's translation keeps the sweep of the march in classic prose. No other ancient account of Alexander matches its completeness and authority.
arrian-anabasis-chinnock:
Arrian, a Greek officer and historian of the Roman era, wrote the Anabasis of Alexander in the second century. E. J. Chinnock translated its seven books into English. Arrian drew on eyewitness accounts now lost to us.

He follows Alexander from his first battles in Asia to his death. Granicus, Issus, Gaugamela, and the march into India unfold in order. Arrian writes as a soldier judging another soldier's craft. Historians still treat his account as the best ancient source on Alexander. Chinnock's version remains plain, steady, and highly readable. Chinnock's translation first appeared in 1884 and long stayed in print.
billy-and-the-big-stick:
Richard Harding Davis sets Billy and the Big Stick in Haiti. Its president, Hamilear Poussevain, called President Ham, revokes the Wilmot Electric Light Company's concession. The company had dared ask payment for lighting Port-au-Prince. Barefoot soldiers surround the power-house. Young Billy Grant, the company's man on the spot, must fight the republic with a cable office and his wits.

Billy warns a Haitian official that he will deliver a copy of his protest to his president first, and returns to the power-house with faithful retainers in tow. Davis, the era's most famous war correspondent, wrote the story as a comic gloss on Roosevelt's big-stick diplomacy. Its Haiti is stage scenery, but the pacing is pure Davis.
by-sheer-pluck: By Sheer Pluck, G. A. Henty's Ashanti War tale. The plucky hero. This book preserves that adventure. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham-van-d:
Abraham van Diepenbeeck was an erudite painter of the Flemish school, born at Bois-le-Duc in 1599 and dead at Antwerp in 1675. After a classical education he became one of Rubens's finest pupils and assistants, handling mythological and historical subjects and portraits with skill and vigour. A sound colourist, he moved to Antwerp about 1629, first winning notice painting on glass, including Acts of Mercy windows in the cathedral.

Admitted to the painters' guild in 1638, he directed the academy from 1641. After a visit to Italy he worked chiefly in oil and illustration. His fifty-eight designs for the Abbe de Marolles' Tableaux du Temple des Muses were engraved by Cornelis Bloemaert. In England under Charles I he painted the Duke of Newcastle's family and illustrated his book on horsemanship. His works hang in the Louvre, Vienna, Munich, Dresden, Berlin, and Brussels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoon-anthon:
Flemish portrait painter Anthony van Dyck, born at Antwerp in 1599 and dead in London in 1641, was the seventh child of a silk and linen merchant. Placed as a boy in the studio of Hendrick van Balen, he developed fast. He painted a likeness of an old man at fourteen and a series of heads later revealed in a lawsuit. Before twenty, in 1618, he was admitted to the membership of the Guild of St. Luke at Antwerp, an unusual honour for so young a painter.

The tradition that he was Rubens's apprentice is dismissed here: he was already a master when he entered Rubens's studio to help with decorative work. The entry traces his early Antwerp years, his precocious skill, and his place among Rubens's young assistants, before his English court career. Readers get a careful sorting of legend from record in a short, brilliant life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bismarck:
Bismarck, a diocese in North Dakota, is the subject of this short 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Erected on the last day of 1909 and suffragan to St. Paul, Minnesota, it covers eighteen counties across 42,316 square miles of prairie. Vincent Wehrle, a Swiss Benedictine of Einsiedeln, became its first bishop in 1910.

Born at Berg in Switzerland in 1855, professed in 1876, and ordained in 1879, Wehrle had laboured among German settlers in the Dakotas before his election. The entry lists parishes, clergy, and schools of a young frontier diocese. It reads as a founding snapshot of Catholic life on the northern plains.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-john-:
Blessed John Ruysbroeck, surnamed the Admirable Doctor, foremost of the Flemish mystics, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Ruysbroeck near Brussels in 1293, he died at Groenendael in 1381. A devout mother trained him from infancy, and at eleven he left home without warning for his uncle John Hinckaert, canon of St. Gudule's at Brussels.

Writing in the Flemish tongue against heretical books spread among the people, he moved with two friends to the hermitage of Groenendael in 1343. Disciples flocked there until the hermitage became a community of canons regular in 1349. His Sparkling Stone and Adornment of the Spiritual Marriage remain classics of mysticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chevalier-de-:
An entry on Jean-Baptiste de Lamarck, the French botanist, zoologist, and natural philosopher known as the Chevalier de Lamarck. Born at Bazentin in Picardy in 1744, he joined the French army in 1761 after his father's death. He was made an officer on the field during the Seven Years' War. Illness forced him out at twenty-four, and he worked as a bank clerk in Paris while studying medicine and plants.

Lamarck never practised medicine, and his writings on weather and chemistry carry no scientific weight. In biology he excelled: able botanist from 1778, zoologist from 1794, and from about 1800 a speculative writer on the variation of species. His Flore française of 1778 gave the first full account of French plants and set out his dichotomous system, a key that sorts species by paired choices. He held that classification must weigh all parts of a plant, not one alone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-communion-of-:
Patrick Morrisroe's entry covers Communion of the sick, which differs from ordinary Communion in persons, dispositions, place, and ceremonies. The Church, anxious for her children's spiritual welfare, will not leave the ill without the sacrament's consolations. Pastors must meet the desires of the dangerously sick, who need strength for the final struggle. They must also meet those who cannot keep the paschal precept in church. They must meet all who hunger for this life-giving bread from mere devotion.

Dispositions get their own section. The sick who receive from devotion were bound to fast beforehand. Ceremonies follow the Roman Ritual, with the priest bearing the sacrament to the house. Morrisroe draws on Catalani, Baruffaldi, O'Kane, Van der Stappen, and Gasparri to set out the rules. The entry serves pastors and families facing illness, showing how the Church brings the altar to the bedside.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-croagh-patric:
This entry describes Croagh Patrick, the cone-shaped mountain on Clew Bay in County Mayo, called the Sinai of Ireland. Rising 2,510 feet above the Atlantic shore, it was known in pagan times as Cruachan Aigli. Its Christian fame rests on St. Patrick's Lent there in 441.

Weary from labour, Patrick climbed the peak on the Saturday before Ash Wednesday to fast, pray, and plead that faith might not fail in Ireland. Tradition tells that God summoned all Ireland's saints, past, present, and future, to console him with a vision of the harvest his work would yield. The entry warns that its sources postdate Patrick by three hundred years, yet argues the traditions they carry are genuine. Pilgrimage continues there to this day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-rock:
A biographical entry presents Daniel Rock, antiquarian and ecclesiologist, born at Liverpool in 1799 and dead at Kensington in 1871. Schooled at Saint Edmund's College, Old Hall, he came under the liturgist Louis Havard and befriended the historian Mark Tierney. Chosen among the first students to reopen the English College at Rome, he took a doctorate there in 1825.

Ordained in 1824, he served at Saint Mary's, Moorfields, then as chaplain to the Earl of Shrewsbury at Alton Towers. His Hierurgia of 1833, on the sacrifice of the Mass, grew from two Roman years of research. His greatest book, The Church of Our Fathers, studies the Sarum Rite and medieval liturgy, and made him England's leading authority on the subject.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eberhard-bill:
Eberhard Billick, also called Steinberger, was a German theologian and foe of the Reformation, born at Cologne in 1499 or 1500. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows him into the Carmelites in 1513, through vows, priesthood, and a readership in divinity, to the priorships of Cassel and Cologne. He took his doctorate in 1540 and in 1542 became provincial of Lower Germany, a post he held until death, though named auxiliary bishop of Cologne too late to be consecrated.

His work for his order thrived, enrolling many candidates, and his writing against Bucer drew the wrath of Luther and Melanchthon. Disputations took him to Worms, Ratisbon, and Augsburg, and in 1551 he attended the Council of Trent as theologian to Cologne's new archbishop. He died at Cologne on 12 January 1557.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edelinck:
Edelinck is the family name of four engravers, chief among them Gerard Edelinck. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how Gerard, born at Antwerp about 1640, learned the rudiments from Galle and drank in the vigor of the Rubens school of engravers. Paris drew him in 1665, where study with de Poilly soon left the master behind and brought him almost at once to his full powers.

Le Brun and Colbert drew Louis the Fourteenth's eye to him. From the king came commissions, a pension, the title of royal engraver, Gobelins rooms, and a professorship there. He pictured the king's features in fourteen engravings, and his powers stayed undimmed until his death at Paris in 1707.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-and-p:
Francis and Peter Kenrick were brothers, Dublin-born archbishops who shaped the Catholic Church in nineteenth-century America, Francis at Baltimore and Peter at St. Louis. Francis Patrick, born 3 December 1797, and Peter, born 17 August 1806, were sons of Thomas Kenrick and Jane. Their uncle, Father Richard Kenrick of St. Nicholas of Myra, Dublin, nurtured the piety he saw early in both boys. At eighteen Francis was chosen to study for the priesthood at Rome, where the gentle bearing of the restored Pius VII left a lasting lesson.

Francis threw himself into Scripture and the Fathers, and his learning later served the American Church against the Nativist and Know-Nothing attacks of his day. Peter built up the vast St. Louis diocese, riding hundreds of miles on visitation and bringing in religious orders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-ove:
Friedrich Overbeck, a convert painter born at Lübeck in 1789, led the Nazarene school that remade German religious art. Trained at the Vienna Academy, he quit its formalism and settled at Rome in 1810 with three friends in the empty Irish Franciscan house of San Isidoro. He held that church art had stalled for three centuries and set out to bridge the gap.

His Joseph frescoes at Casa Bartholdi, his Tasso scenes at Villa Massimo, and his Miracle of Roses at Assisi won praise for fresh technique and for fitting painting to architecture. His Triumph of Religion in the Arts still hangs at Frankfurt's Städel Gallery. Through pupils like Steinle, and through France, Belgium, Poland, and Spain, his spirit spread well beyond Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-leo-ha:
George Leo Haydock, a priest and Biblical scholar born in Lancashire in 1774, gave English Catholics their enduring Douay Bible. Schooled at Douai, he fled the Revolution in August 1793 with his brother Thomas and reached Crook Hall by 1796. Ordained in September 1798, he served poor missions at Ugthorpe and Whitby, then Westby Hall, where a clash with superiors cost him his faculties in 1831.

Eight years of study at the Tagg followed, with two appeals to Rome intercepted, until a third appeal in 1838 restored him and sent him to Penrith for his last decade. His chief work re-edited Challoner's text of the English Vulgate, issued at Manchester in 1812 to 1814 and reprinted into the 1850s. He also wrote The Tree of Life, prayer books, hymns, and Sabbath meditations, leaving further biblical manuscripts unpublished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giles-de-coni:
Giles de Coninck, also called Regius, was a Jesuit theologian born at Bailleul in French Flanders in 1571, who died at Louvain in 1633. He entered the Society of Jesus at twenty-one and studied at Louvain under Lessius. He then succeeded his teacher in the chair of scholastic theology, which he held for eighteen years. A Catholic Encyclopedia article praises his concise, clear, and direct style.

St. Alphonsus ranked him a moral theologian of distinction, though de Lugo attacked his views on many points. His chief work, a commentary and disputations on the whole teaching of St. Thomas, appeared at Antwerp in 1616 and ran through many editions. A later Rouen edition was condemned to be torn and burnt by the parliament there in 1762. His treatise on the morality of supernatural acts and his posthumous disputations round out his output.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-bruc:
Mainz bishop Heinrich Brück, born at Bingen in 1831, rose from the cooper's trade to the chair of church history and the episcopate. Taught by Dr. Hirschel, trained at Mainz seminary, ordained in 1855, and polished at Munich under Döllinger and in Rome, taught church history at Mainz from 1867. He taught there except during the seminary's closure from 1878 to 1887.

Canon in 1889 and bishop in 1899, he ruled Mainz with zeal until 1903. His fame rests on books. A church history manual of 1874 was translated into English, French, and Italian. A five-volume history of the Catholic Church in Germany in the nineteenth century was praised for thoroughness and sound judgment. Beside them stand lives, a study of rationalism, and a study of Spain's secret societies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-wang:
Munich Jesuit Heinrich Wangnereck, born in 1595, taught philosophy and theology at Dillingen for most of his life and served as its chancellor for twenty-four years by one account. Entering the Society at sixteen at Landsberg, he also taught the lowest gymnasium class and preached widely. He spent 1655 to 1660 as superior and missioner at Lindau before returning to Dillingen, where apoplexy at table killed him in 1664.

Princes, bishops, and prelates across Germany sought his advice, and twenty known works, chiefly theological, include a 1630 commentary on St. Augustine's Confessions still popular in a fourth edition of 1907. He also entered the political controversies of his day, once punished by his general for speaking disrespectfully of the Duke of Bavaria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hubert-and-ja:
Hubert and Jan van Eyck were Flemish brothers, illuminators and painters who founded the school of Bruges and thus all the painting schools of northern Europe. Hubert was born at Maeseyck about 1366, and Jan about twenty years later. Their sister Margaret won fame as a miniaturist. The earliest mention of a Hubert painting dates to 1413.

Hubert lived at Ghent by 1424 and died there in 1426. Jan presented a Madonna's head to Antwerp's guild in 1420, decorated a paschal candle for Cambrai in 1422, and served Jean Sans Merci at The Hague in 1425. Later he joined Philip the Good of Burgundy as painter and chamberlain. He travelled to Portugal to paint Isabella's portrait true to life for Philip's marriage choice, and settled at Bruges, where his art reshaped northern painting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-chadwic:
Second bishop of Hexham and Newcastle, James Chadwick was born at Drogheda, Ireland, on 24 April 1813, and died at Newcastle on 14 May 1882, buried at Ushaw. His father John Chadwick was a gentleman of an old Catholic Lancashire family settled in Ireland, and his mother was Frances Dromgoole. He was educated at Ushaw College from May 1825 until his ordination on 17 December 1836.

Ushaw kept him for years after ordination: three as general prefect, then as teacher of humanities, then five years as philosophy professor. The vice-presidency of the college and the chair of dogmatic theology came in 1849, but within a few months his health broke down. Recovery came among secular priests devoted to preaching missions and retreats, and after fire destroyed their Wooler house in 1856 he returned to Ushaw as philosophy professor. The entry follows a college man toward the episcopate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-eck:
Johann Eck, theologian and Luther's chief adversary, was born at Eck in Swabia in 1486 and died at Ingolstadt in 1543. His family name was Maier, his father a town magistrate, and Johann took Eckius from his birthplace after 1505. His uncle at Rothenburg schooled him from 1495.

Admitted to Heidelberg at twelve, Eck took arts master's at Tübingen in 1501. He studied at Cologne and Freiburg, adding law, physics, maths, geography, Hebrew, and Greek to philosophy and theology. Tutoring his way after his uncle cut funds, he became rector of Freiburg's arts hall in 1505. He took bachelor of theology, lecturer on the Sentences, licentiate in 1509, and doctor at twenty-four in 1510, ordained in 1508.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-alcock:
John Alcock was an English bishop, statesman, and builder who founded Jesus College, Cambridge. Born at Beverley in 1430, he studied at Cambridge, held the rectory of St. Margaret's in London and the deanery of St. Stephen's, Westminster, and became Master of the Rolls in 1462 and privy councillor in 1470. He served on commissions treating with Scotland and was tutor to the young King Edward V.

As bishop successively of Rochester, Worcester, and Ely, he restored many church buildings and was buried in a fine chapel he had built for himself in Ely Cathedral. His writings include the Sponsage of a Virgin to Christ, the Hill of Perfection, sermons on Luke's eighth chapter, and translations from the French. Bale praised his virtue and sanctity, and he founded Jesus College on the site of a ruined nunnery, endowing Peterhouse as well.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-mullock:
John Mullock was the Franciscan Bishop of St. John's, Newfoundland, who championed its fisheries, resources, and the Atlantic cable. Born at Limerick in 1807, he studied at Seville and at St. Isidore's in Rome, where he was ordained in 1830, served long in Ireland, and became coadjutor of St. John's in 1847, succeeding Bishop Fleming in 1850.

Under him the Church grew rapidly, a new diocese of Harbour Grace was erected, and the splendid St. John's cathedral, begun in 1841, was consecrated in 1855. Keen on Newfoundland's commercial development, he advised governors on fisheries and other matters. Long before the first cable attempt of 1857 he publicly argued that Europe and America could be joined by submarine telegraph. He also introduced English readers to St. Alphonsus Liguori with a life in 1846 and a translation of his History of Heresies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-nepomuk-:
John Nepomuk Tschupick was a celebrated Viennese court preacher of the eighteenth century. Born at Vienna in 1729, he entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1744 and soon taught grammar and rhetoric. In 1763 he became preacher at Vienna cathedral, a post he filled for the last twenty-two years of his life, marked by exceptional conscientiousness, prudence, and ability.

His preaching won the high appreciation of Francis I, Maria Theresa, Joseph II, and the imperial court. His sermons stood out for clear, logical thought and precise, forceful expression, and copious, skillful use of patristic and biblical texts. His sermons were collected in ten small volumes with an index at Vienna in 1785 to 1787. They were supplemented by new sermons in 1798 to 1803, re-edited in five volumes at Paderborn, and translated into Italian. They kept his reputation long after his death in 1784.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kasper-franck: This 1913 reference piece on Franck — a German writer of note. Henry Joseph Schroeder surveys his works. Little survives about his life. The sixteenth century was his time. The learned press knew his pen. His 1590 works are famed. His 1590 writings are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lawrence-beye: A 1913 entry on Beyerlinck — the Antwerp canonist. John Bertram Peterson honors his famous works. His pen served the learned schools. The chapter prized its learned son. The seventeenth century knew his name. His 1627 death is famed. His 1627 works are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-limerick: This 1913 reference article on Limerick — the Irish diocese. Edward D'Alton gives its ancient story. Its bishops guard the Shannon flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the Erin's west. Its 12th-century see is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-little-rock: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Little Rock — the Arkansas diocese. John Lucey gives its founding story. Its bishops guard the southern flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the American south. Its 1843 founding is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lubeck: This 1913 reference article on Lübeck — the Hanseatic diocese. Joseph Lins gives its ancient story. Its bishops guard the Baltic flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the German north. Its 12th-century see is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maurice-cleno: A 1913 entry on Clenock — the Welsh martyr. Edwin Burton unfolds his fateful tale. He sealed the faith with blood. Erin keeps the holy name. The sixteenth century knew his death. His 1581 death is famed. His 1581 martyrdom is famed. His 1581 Tyburn martyrdom is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melchior-baro: A 1913 entry on Diepenbrock — the Breslau cardinal. Boniface Luebbermann honors his famous see. His prudence steered the Silesian Church. The pope prized the able son. The nineteenth century knew his name. His 1853 death is famed. His 1845 Breslau is famed. His 1845 Silesian see is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-osnabrueck: Osnabrück, the Westphalian city of the famous peace, kept its prince-bishopric through the Reformation's storms. This entry covers its diocese, its bishops, and its history. The city of the Peace of Westphalia: its bishops bridged the confessions after the wars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-lambeck: Peter Lambeck was the imperial librarian of Vienna whose histories preserved the Habsburg collections. This entry covers his career, his catalogues, and his scholarship. The keeper of the emperor's books: his learned catalogues mapped the vast imperial library of old Vienna.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-plock: Płock, the ancient Polish city of the Vistula, became a diocese. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The Church in the city of the Mazovian dukes: its noble cathedral crowns the high Vistula bluff high above the river.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reginald-peco: Reginald Pecock was the bishop who wrote in English. This entry notes his books, his trial, and his recantation. The prelate of the vernacular: his plain English stirred the angry bishops of London's court in 1457's cold winter of trial.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sebastian-von: Sebastian von Rostock was the bishop of Breslau. This entry notes his see, his age, and his works. The prelate of the Silesian church: his princely see crowned Breslau in Silesia's capital in the 1660s' empire in the north of the Reich.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seven-branch-: The seven-branch candlestick is the lamp of the Temple. This entry explains its form, its meaning, and its history. The menorah of the holy place: its seven lamps lit the Temple in Jerusalem's sanctuary in the Holy of Holies in the Bible.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-ch: The Sisters of Charity of St. John are the daughters of New Brunswick. This entry covers their rule, their schools, and their houses. The sisters of the Bay of Fundy: their many schools dot the diocese in the 1850s' decades.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-nicholas-p: St. Nicholas Pieck was the Franciscan martyr of Gorkum. This entry traces his Brielle, his constancy, and his crown. The guardian of the Dutch friars: his martyr's blood sealed Brielle in the 1572 of the Geuzen in the town of the Maas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-patrick: St. Patrick was the apostle of Ireland. This very long entry examines his Confession, his Armagh, and his fame. The patron of the Irish nation: his great see crowned Armagh in the 400s' Ulster in the north of the province.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-simon-stoc: St. Simon Stock was the Carmelite of the scapular. This entry traces his Aylesford, his Mary, and his fame. The general of the English friars: his brown scapular crowned Aylesford in the 1250s' Kent in the Medway of the river.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-august: Hendrick was the bishop of Cebu. This entry traces his 1800s, his Philippines, and his see. The prelate of the island diocese: his new Cebu crowned the Philippines in the 1900s of the Americans in the truly very old islands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-sedgwi: Sedgwick was the martyr of the north. This entry traces his 1500s, his seminary, and his death. The priest of the English mission: his brave death crowned the north in the 1580s of the mission in the very old moors.
doe-osti-2575077-pfas-removal-by-ion-exc: PFAS removal by ion exchange got its Hanford review, and this DOE report covers background and knowledge gaps. The pages detail the resin science. The cleanup crews get their briefing. The site was Hanford. The resins were ion exchange. The science was resin.
doe-osti-2589585-low-swap-trapped-ion-at: Trapped ion atomic clocks got their low SWaP, and this DOE report covers the compact design. The pages detail the engineering. The timing folks get their device. The clock was trapped ion. The design was compact. The folks were timing.
doe-osti-3029333-final-technical-report-: Quantum black holes got finally reported, and this DOE technical report covers wormholes. The pages detail the findings. The physicists get their closeout. The report was final technical. The closeout was physicist. The wormholes were holes. The holes were black.
galen-natural-faculties-brock:
Arthur J. Brock translated Galen's On the Natural Faculties for the Loeb series in 1916. Galen, antiquity's greatest doctor after Hippocrates, wrote the treatise around 175 CE. It became the foundational text of ancient physiology for centuries.

Galen holds that each organ has purpose-built powers of its own. The stomach attracts, retains, alters, and expels food by distinct faculties. Kidneys, liver, and blood vessels each work by similar natural powers. His system ruled medicine for some fourteen hundred years afterward. Brock's Loeb gives Greek facing English for students. Modern physiology replaced Galen's faculties, but his reasoning shaped medicine's very questions.
gobseck:
Honore de Balzac's Gobseck, translated by Ellen Marriage, opens at one in the morning in the winter of 1829-30, in the Vicomtesse de Grandlieu's salon, where the lawyer Derville tells a story. Its subject is Gobseck, the Dutch moneylender, a pupil of Balzac's own Vendome schoolfellow's dedication reminds readers, rendered as philosophy with a cash box. Gobseck lends to desperate aristocrats and watches Paris through its debts.

The Countess de Restaud burns papers in the grate as Derville approaches, fearing a will that disinherits her children, while Gobseck savors his one laugh at the expense of the ruined. Balzac returns to Gobseck across the Comedie humaine; this tale is the usurer's fullest portrait, terrifying and oddly admiring.
good-luck: Good Luck, by L, t, meade, the luck's tale. This book preserves that children's story. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
govdocs-archive_org-LiturgicalShipwreck_:
Michael Davies, an English Catholic traditionalist writer, published Liturgical Shipwreck in the 1990s, marking twenty-five years of the reformed Roman Mass, 1969 to 1994. Davies defended the old Latin rite against the changes that followed the Second Vatican Council. His books armed traditionalists worldwide.

He argues that the new Mass broke with the faith the old rite expressed, and that the wreck of the liturgy wrecked belief itself. Davies marshals texts, translations, and the reformers' own words in a lawyerly case. The book is Catholic traditionalism's argument fully made, of record for readers on any side of the liturgy wars.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BrookingJack_Br: 'Rest Stop III' by Jack Brooking (Jack Beach): the declassified government document - the work as captured. Subject: government records. A bare holding, preserved as released. An obscure item, complete. From the archive's collection, for researchers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FrazierJack_Fra: Jack Frazier: the badly garbled letter apparently concerning dental documents and Oswald's contacts. Damaged, but kept, complete. A single letter. An obscure item, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GougglemanTucke:
Murrey Marder reported for the Washington Post that three Americans were still being held in Vietnam. Among them was a former official of the Central Intelligence Agency. A fourth American had reached Bangkok, which is how word of the others came out.

Men held after a war ends become a slow diplomatic wound. Families wait, governments negotiate in private, and newspapers keep the names alive. Marder's article preserves the state of that captivity as the Post reported it, with one man free in Bangkok and three prisoners still inside Vietnam, their names kept before the public.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LawrenceJack_La:
In January 1964, the FBI's Pittsburgh office sent this airtel to the Dallas office about Lee Harvey Oswald. The file heading was 'IS-R-Cuba,' the bureau's internal-security label for the Oswald case. Special Agent Leon R. Graben reported his attempts to reach a subject in Charleston, West Virginia.

Airtels were the bureau's fast internal messages, and thousands of them built the Oswald file. Most record small errands like this one: an agent sent to find a person, a visit made, a lead checked. Together they show the scale of the inquiry that followed the assassination, reaching into cities far from Dallas and pulling in people who had only glancing contact with the case.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NobleNick_Noble:
Harold Weisberg wrote this letter on January 12, 1976, to a Mr. Noble. Its subjects are practical ones. Weisberg discusses the government documents reproduced in his books, and what transcripts cost him to obtain. He also raises Senator Richard Russell's unrecorded doubts about the official account.

Russell had served on the Warren Commission, and researchers believed he had dissented in private. Weisberg chased that belief for years. The letter to Noble mixes that chase with the bookkeeping of self-publishing: documents bought, pages copied, costs counted. It is a working letter from a man running a one-man research institute out of his house, and it shows both halves of that enterprise.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PickupTruck_Pic:
An FBI report dated December 24, 1963 records an account by J. D. LeFlore. LeFlore described a green Chevrolet pickup truck seen stopped in front of the Texas School Book Depository before the motorcade arrived. The truck carried lettering for 'air conditioning' on its side.

Witness reports of strange vehicles fill the early assassination files. Each was logged, however small, because no one yet knew which details mattered. A lettered truck in front of the building an hour before the shooting was exactly the sort of thing agents were told to chase. The report preserves LeFlore's description, the date it was taken, and the bureau's decision to keep it in the record.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WaiteJack_Waite: A letter reached Harold Weisberg from Philadelphia on October 20, 1966. The writer mentions work under way and the rechecking of facts. Weisberg drew letters from readers and fellow researchers across the country as his books appeared. The Philadelphia letter is one piece of that early network, when assassination research still moved mostly by mail between people who had never met.
joe-the-hotel-boy-or-winning-out-by-pluc:
Joe the Hotel Boy, or Winning Out by Pluck, is a boys' novel by Horatio Alger Jr. The contents run to thirty chapters, from Out in a Storm to a closing Conclusion. In his preface, Alger recalls his long series about boys who make their own way in the world. Newsboys, match boys, peddlers, and street musicians filled the earlier books.

Joe's story turns on a search for a blue box, named again and again in the chapter titles. Along the way come a ruined home, an accident on the lake, a swindle, and a fire at the hotel. Joe visits Chicago, makes a discovery, and sees two evildoers meet their fate. Alger's formula holds: pluck, honesty, and hard work carry a poor boy upward.
master-humphrey-s-clock:
Charles Dickens built Master Humphrey's Clock round an old man and his clock. He gave the book to the poet Samuel Rogers in 1840. His first note to readers is dated April 4, 1840.

Master Humphrey hopes all sorts of readers find cheer in his clock. Dickens says the parts would come out week by week. He trusts the clock's voice to lighten the hours it counts. The frame lets friends meet, tell tales, and share the passing time. A preface to the first volume follows the short address. Dickens frames short tales as gifts left in an old man's clock case.
mistress-penwick:
Dutton Payne's romance opens, by its contents, as the Ursuline convent loses a pupil. The Lord of Crandlemar and a ball follow, then his lordship's proposal. Janet's philosophy and a chapter called The Brantle deepen the intrigue. Sir Julian Pomphrey and a Jacques Dempsy enter the cast.

Later chapters move between castle and ancient monastery. Something happens in the butlery, and nine tolls from the chapel belfry. Sermons new and old close the contents list. Payne builds a tale of convent girlhood, aristocratic courtship, and old buildings full of secrets, in the manner of the period's historical romances.
mr-prohack:
Arnold Bennett's novel follows Arthur Charles Prohack, a calm man who hates to be hurried. Chapter one, The New Poor, finds him at breakfast at eight thirty. The contents promise law, family strain, idleness, and a yacht. Two children, Charlie and Sissie, share the stage with his wife Eve.

Bennett traces how new wealth and new poverty test one household. Prohack tries rest, travel, and doing nothing at all. Eve and the children pull him back into real life. The tone is wry and close to daily detail. It is a study of money, work, and middle age in modern London.
mr-waddington-of-wyck:
May Sinclair published this novel in 1921, set at Lower Wyck Manor. Fanny Waddington drifts in and out with tulips for old bowls. She hums as she works and seems light as a butterfly. Young Barbara Madden watches her during her first days there.

Barbara is new to the house and learns its ways fast. She notes the Tudor windows, the garden, and the stores lists. Mr. Waddington of the title rules this calm world. Sinclair studies marriage and self-deceit in a quiet key. Small acts and soft talk reveal the strain beneath the manor's peace.
nasa-tm-19700024994-crew-egress-procedur:
Dated December 7, 1966, this Houston working paper gives crew escape procedures for the Apollo Block I command module at sea. After a splashdown or a pad abort into water, the crew had to get out of the floating capsule.

The paper opens with a summary and an introduction. It then lays out the steps for leaving the craft in the open sea. Block I capsules were an early design used for ground and early flight tests. Clear escape steps, written before flight, gave crews a practiced path out. That mattered most when a capsule sat low in rough water.
on-horseback:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote this travel book about the South. The ride begins at Abingdon in southwest Virginia. A professor gives a comic lesson on mounting a horse. The horse steps around and faces him mid lesson. Townsfolk watch from cane chairs before the hotel.

Warner rides through North Carolina and East Tennessee. The professor can recite Chaucer's tales while trotting, Warner jokes. Abingdon keeps old tobacco wealth and easy habits, he notes. Warner mixes humor, scenery, and social comment. The book preserves Southern life after the Civil War. The town holds the Stonewall Jackson Institute in its midst. The late Floyd home now serves as a school for girls.
on-the-track:
Henry Lawson published these Australian stories in Sydney in 1900. His preface is dated March 17 of that year. Many tales first ran in various periodicals, he notes. Several appear in print here for the first time. The contents name swagman Mitchell in many tales.

Stories treat matrimony, jobs, women, and old mates. A ventriloquial rooster and bush cats add dry humor. The first tale recalls songs sung on the diggings. Lambing Flat and Gulgong name old gold rush camps. His tales voice Australia's frontier with humor and heartbreak. The contents also list Andy Page's Rival and the Iron-Bark Chip. Home Rule joins the list of old diggings named.
orange-and-green-a-tale-of-the-boyne-and:
G. A. Henty set his boys' novel Orange and Green in the Irish war of 1689 to 1691, when the deposed King James fought William of Orange for the crown. The story runs from a shipwreck through the siege and relief of Derry, the battle of the Boyne, and the sieges of Limerick, ending in peace. Orange and green name the two camps, Protestant and Catholic Irish.

In his preface Henty explains the grievance behind the war: Irish land taken from its owners and given to Cromwell's followers, and what remained preyed on by greedy intriguers. He says he drew most heavily on Irish accounts so his young readers would see events from the Irish point of view. The novel mixes that history lesson with cavalry raids, winter quarters, and dangerous missions.
passing-of-the-third-floor-back:
Jerome K. Jerome's story opens on a November afternoon near Bloomsbury Square in London. A stranger with an odd, curved back and a young face draws the notice of everyone he passes, a newsboy, a nursemaid, and a constable. Copyrighted in 1904, the tale became one of Jerome's best-loved works.

The stranger takes the shabby third-floor back room in a boarding house full of selfish, quarrelling lodgers. His quiet presence slowly changes each of them for the better. Gentle and a little mystical, the story suggests that one good person can redeem a whole household.
peshitta-new-testament-murdock:
James Murdock, an American scholar of Syriac, published his English New Testament from the Syriac Peshitta in 1852. The Peshitta is the Bible of the Syriac-speaking churches of the East, in use since the early centuries of the faith. Murdock's was the earliest widely used English rendering of that version.

Reading the Gospels and letters in Syriac dress gives small shocks: names, phrases, and some whole verses shift from the Greek-based texts most readers know. The Peshitta also lacks a few books found in Western Bibles. Murdock kept notes on the main differences as they came. His version opened the Eastern church's scripture to English readers.
philosopher-jack:
R. M. Ballantyne's Philosopher Jack, dated 1879 in this record, opens with a strange friendship. Jack, whose other name is Edwin, is a nineteen-year-old student of argumentative mind. His most intimate friend never says anything to him beyond two words: Don't, and Do. The friend's name, the reader learns, is Conscience.

A letter from Jack's father then destroys his prospects: bad seasons have emptied the farm purse, and the golden gates of knowledge close. Jack asks himself whether to go to sea, and Conscience says Don't. Ballantyne's tale follows the impulsive philosopher who asks the question anyway: for what end was I created?
podcast-tuckercarlson-2VXbY4V7LCk:
John Mearsheimer, the political scientist known for realist theory and blunt talk, joins Tucker Carlson to argue that Israel's war in Gaza amounts to genocide against Palestinians. His charge goes further: he says the West has been deceived into supporting it, and he names the mechanisms of that deception.

Mearsheimer has criticized American foreign policy for decades, and Carlson gives him an unhurried hearing rare on television. The two discuss media coverage, lobbying, and the strategic cost to the United States. The claims are the speakers' own and remain fiercely disputed, but the episode preserves a prominent scholar making the case directly. Listeners get the argument unfiltered, which is the stated point of the program.
podcast-tuckercarlson-6PdWKkyooCk:
Laura Delano spent years as a psychiatric patient, taking the medications prescribed for her diagnoses, before she concluded the system itself had harmed her. With Tucker Carlson, she argues that the drug industry created the modern mental health crisis and profits from keeping it permanent.

Delano now works with people trying to leave psychiatric drugs safely, and she describes that process and its dangers in detail. Carlson connects her story to his broader case against pharmaceutical power. Her claims are disputed by much of the medical establishment, and withdrawal from such medication carries real risks she herself stresses. The episode preserves a prominent critic's account in her own words, useful for listeners weighing the system's failures against its defenders' answers.
poor-jack:
Captain Frederick Marryat wrote Poor Jack, presented here as volume ten of his collected works with illustrations. Marryat, a post-captain in the Royal Navy turned novelist, knew the sea from boyhood. This story follows a Greenwich waterman's son who rises through the naval world of the Napoleonic wars. The illustration list alone charts the voyage: Fisher's Alley, Anderson reading the Bible to Jack. News of the battle of the Nile, a French port, a prison, an escape, and a wreck.

Jack's father, a disabled pensioner, and old Bramble, the one-legged sailor who mentors the boy, anchor the shore chapters. Marryat mixes dockside comedy with real seamanship, storms, privateers, and impressment, all drawn from life. Poor Jack was among his most popular tales, a boys' classic that also preserves, in its slang and detail, the vanished world of the Thames watermen and the wooden navy.
poor-man-s-rock:
Bertrand W. Sinclair published Poor Man's Rock in Boston with Little, Brown in September 1920, adding it to his shelf of British Columbia novels beside North of Fifty-Three and Big Timber. A prologue reaches back long, long ago, and the chapters settle in Cradle Bay, among salmon fishermen whose living depends on the runs. Titles such as Vested Rights, the Complexity of Simple Matters, and Sea Boots and Salmon announce the fight: small independent fishermen against the cannery interests that claimed the coast.

Sinclair wrote the Pacific Northwest from inside, having fished and logged it himself, and his fiction argues for the little man with the gillnet against companies with lawyers. The rock of the title is the poor man's foothold, a fishing spot the independents could still work. As a document of the salmon wars and as a rattling regional novel, the book holds both grounds at once.
ralestone-luck: Ralestone Luck, by André Norton, author of The Prince Commands, was published in New York by D. Appleton-Century Company in 1938, with illustrations by James Reid, and dedicated to D. B. N. for miles of proofreading. The pages shown give the frontispiece and first contents: Rupert asks Val the old question, "How hold ye Lorne?" and the contents open with The Ralestones Come Home, The Luck of the Lords of Lorne, and Pistols for Two, Coffee for One.
rhymes-of-a-roughneck:
Pat O'Cotter published these rhymes in 1918 and dedicated the book to Alaska, in a verse of rough praise. Alaska is the home of the tin can and dog, he writes, a waste of snow, ice, and moss. Men come there for gold and stick because they cannot get away; they dig, drink, and die.

The contents open with The Birth of the Land and A Woman, A Dog, and A Walnut Tree. The Throwback, The Malamute, and The Prospector name stock figures of the gold country. When the Water Starts to Run and That 30 U.S. on the Wall close the list, in verse as plain and hard as its subject.
struggling-upward-or-luke-larkin-s-luck:
Horatio Alger Jr. wrote Struggling Upward, or Luke Larkin's Luck, one of his many tales of a poor boy rising by honesty and pluck. Chapter I, The Waterbury Watch, opens on a January Saturday at a pond in the village of Groveton.

A young teacher, Frederic Hooper, a recent Yale graduate, offers a Waterbury watch as prize to the boy who skates across the pond and back in the least time. Among the racers stands Randolph Duncan. He is the spoiled son of Prince Duncan, the rich bank president. The contest sets the pattern Alger's readers knew. Wealth and pride stand on one side. A deserving poor boy stands on the other. Luck rewards steady conduct.
the-adventures-of-johnny-chuck: Thornton W. Burgess wrote The Adventures of Johnny Chuck. It is one of his Bedtime Story Books. Chapters track Johnny from the spring's first days. Gentle Sister South Wind arrives first. Callers then come to Johnny's door. The singers of the Smiling Pool draw him next. He finds out who the sweet singers are. A bout of discontent then takes him. He turns tramp and meets a strange chuck. Love and house hunting with Polly Chuck follow. A new home at last closes the list.
the-adventures-of-poor-mrs-quack: Thornton W. Burgess wrote The Adventures of Poor Mrs. Quack for his Bedtime Story-Books, with art by Harrison Cady. Chapters listed track Peter Rabbit's first meeting with Mrs. Quack at the Smiling Pool, her tale of home and troubles, the terrible guns on her flight south, a hunt for the lost Mr. Quack, and Sammy Jay's plan to help her.
the-auction-block:
Rex Beach wrote the novel, naming Peter Knight and his son James, called Jimmy, in its first pages. Peter, a plump and good-natured Democrat in the small town of Vale, argues with his son about local politics and reform. James urges a move to New York, while his father insists he likes Vale, where everyone knows him.

That opening clash sets up a story of ambition, family strain, and city temptation. James treats his father's standing as a reason to leave, not to stay. Beach, also named on the title page for The Silver Horde and The Spoilers, builds the tale from small-town talk toward larger stakes in New York life.
the-cruise-of-the-dry-dock: T. S. Stribling's The Cruise of the Dry Dock, dated 1917 with pictures by Herbert Morton Stoops, is dedicated to the author's mother. Its contents promise adventure in twenty-two chapters: The Last of the Vulcan, The Mystery Ship, A Modern Columbus, The Sea Serpent, Chased by a Submarine, and The Victoria Cross. A lad named Caradoc shows his mettle and takes command along the way. The picture list shows the heroes under a schooner's overhang. Only the front matter, contents, and picture list are present here.
the-cuckoo-clock: Mrs. Molesworth, author of Herr Baby and Carrots, wrote The Cuckoo Clock, printed in London by Macmillan in 1895 with pictures by Walter Crane. A dedication dated from Edinburgh in 1877 names Mary Josephine and the dear memory of her brother Thomas Grindal, both called friendly little critics of the author's stories for children. The contents begin with a chapter called The Old House. Only the front matter and the start of the contents are present here.
the-eight-strokes-of-the-clock:
Maurice Le Blanc's The Eight Strokes of the Clock, dated 1923 in its front pages, holds eight Arsène Lupin tales. Le Blanc's note says Lupin told him these feats as a friend's, one Prince Rénine, yet the hero's acts and mind look so much like Lupin's own that the two seem one. Titles name a water bottle, a tell-tale film, and footprints in the snow.

The first tale opens atop a tower, with Hortense Daniel calling down to a fat man in the shrubs. Rénine solves each case with nerve, charm, and a magician's timing.
the-garden-of-the-plynck:
Karle Wilson Baker wrote The Garden of the Plynck as a tale for children, with Sara at its heart. Ten chapters move from a dimple smithy to Sara's day.

The tale opens by teasing grown folk who start tales with when I was a little girl, then turn the tale into a scolding. Sara's mother, dear but busy and contrary, darns, writes, and reads dark books with no pictures. Against that plain world stands the Plynck's garden, a place of odd folk and small wonders. Baker mixes wit for grown readers with a child's world a step off the real one.
the-hunchback:
James Sheridan Knowles wrote the two plays in this volume. The Hunchback and The Love-Chase appear together. Cassell published the edition in 1887. The introduction traces an unlikely career. Knowles was born at Cork in 1784. His father taught elocution and compiled a dictionary. The boy took an army commission. He gave it up for the stage. Acting brought him no greatness. He taught elocution at Belfast and Glasgow instead. His first play appeared at Belfast in 1815.

Everything changed through the actor Macready. Virginius had succeeded at Glasgow. A friend pressed the manuscript on the rising tragedian. Macready read it unwillingly in April 1820. He finished it in a state of excitement. The fresh dialogue and passionate scenes absorbed him. Knowles became Macready's own poet after that. His real gift was building situations for actors. A fine performer could move an audience through them.
the-legends-of-saint-patrick:
Aubrey de Vere wrote verse legends of Saint Patrick first published in 1872, and Cassell issued this small edition in London in 1892. An introduction traces poetic gift from Sir Aubrey de Vere to his third son, born in 1814. Sir Aubrey sonnets won high praise from Wordsworth, the editor notes.

The younger de Vere wrote noble verse tied to love of God, man, and Ireland across a long life. His Patrick legends retell the saint missions, wonders, and prayers in lyric and narrative poems. The editor chose this book from three collected volumes of his verse.
the-life-and-adventures-of-kit-carson-th: De Witt C. Peters wrote his life of Kit Carson from facts Carson narrated himself, and New York publishers issued it in 1858. Only the title page and the start of a dedication letter to Colonel Ceran St. Vrain of New Mexico are present here. The letter calls St. Vrain the first mountaineer to spot and guide Carson energy, ability, and courage. The adventures themselves, across the Rocky Mountains and the far West, remain outside this record.
the-mayor-of-warwick: Herbert M. Hopkins, author of The Fighting Bishop, published The Mayor of Warwick with Houghton, Mifflin and Company in April 1906. Only the title page, a dedication to Pauline, and the contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. Chapter titles promise a meeting in the Maple Walk, a bishop's daughter, a candidate, and star-gazers. Later chapters turn to a confession, the president taking a hand, and the blindness of the bishop.
the-moon-rock:
Arthur J. Rees's 1922 novel The Moon Rock opens with an epigraph from Swinburne on a bitter world, then moves to a funeral in Cornwall. Chapter I buries Mrs. Turold in a bleak Cornish churchyard, among strangers and far from her birthplace and kin. The narrator remarks that she had been a nonentity in life and was no less in death.

Her husband lingers alone at the open grave, ignoring the waiting grave-digger. His long, narrow face shows care rather than grief, and his gaze is that of a man sunk in anxious thought. Six mourners wait by a stone cross: four men, a woman, and the dead woman's daughter, whose lovely, sorrowful face turns away from the grave toward the distant sea.
the-norsk-nightingale-being-the-lyrics-o: William F. Kirk published a book of comic verse in 1905, described as the lyrics of a "lumberyack," using Scandinavian immigrant dialect for humor. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the poems themselves do not appear. The lyrics include pieces such as "Yim," Tillie Olson, and a sonnet on stewed prunes. The historical tales retell Horatius at the Bridge, William Tell, Robinson Crusoe, and Paul Revere.
the-purgatory-of-st-patrick:
Denis Florence Mac-Carthy translated Calderon's dramas into English in the metre of the original, publishing at London in 1873 with Henry S. King and Company. The introduction singles out Life Is a Dream as the most celebrated of Calderon's plays, staged across Europe and rendered into many languages.

Mac-Carthy stresses completeness and closeness. Every speech is kept, line for line, in the varied verse forms of the Spanish text, improving on earlier partial versions in blank verse or selected scenes. The title drama concerns Saint Patrick's Purgatory, and readers interested in Spanish theatre gain a full metrical rendering rather than a loose adaptation.
the-story-and-song-of-black-roderick:
Dora Sigerson published this Irish tale in prose and verse in 1906. She announces its subject at once. Black Earl Roderick is its hero. The tale covers his pride and his humbling. It covers the bitterness of his heart and the love that reached him at last. His threatened ruin and his strange rescue close the list.

Roderick leaves his gray castle at dawn on his wedding day. A hundred knights ride with him. They go steady and slow, as if to meet sorrow. No man dares sing or jest behind him. Song stanzas describe his heavy frown and sneer. Only Mora of the Knowledge speaks a warning. She picks herbs in a lonely place. She whispers about the white doe he would kill. Then a honeybee stings his cheek on the road.
the-story-of-a-monkey-on-a-stick: Laura Lee Hope's Make Believe story of a monkey on a stick was published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York, illustrated by Harry L. Smith, with a frontispiece showing the Monkey shaking paws with the Candy Rabbit. Only the title pages and publisher's lists are present here. The lists group the book with the Sawdust Doll. The White Rocking Horse and the Calico Clown stand beside it. A Bobbsey Twins list opens after. The monkey's own adventures do not appear.
the-tale-of-jemima-puddle-duck:
Frederick Warne issued Beatrix Potter's Jemima Puddle-Duck in 1908, billed on its opening page as a farmyard tale for Ralph and Betsy. Jemima is annoyed because the farmer's wife will not let her hatch her own eggs. Her sister-in-law Rebeccah cheerfully admits she lacks the patience to brood eggs for nearly a month. Jemima insists she will hatch her eggs all by herself.

She tries to hide her eggs, yet they are always found and carried off, and she grows quite desperate. Potter sets up a determined mother duck against a practical farm household. The opening promises a secret nest, a risky plan, and trouble ahead for a bird who wants things her own way.
the-tapestried-chamber-and-death-of-the-:
Sir Walter Scott frames The Tapestried Chamber as a story told to him years earlier by Miss Anna Seward, whose spoken tales outshone her written ones. The piece first appeared in The Keepsake of 1828. Scott warns that stories of the marvellous lose force in print compared with a voice lowered beside a fireside. He presents the narrative much as he heard it, avoiding ornament that would spoil its simplicity.

The tale itself, also called The Lady in the Sacque, concerns a haunted room in an old house. Scott's introduction doubles as a small essay on why ghost stories work best when told aloud. Readers get both a classic haunting and a great storyteller explaining his craft before the fright begins.
the-wreck:
The Wreck, copyrighted by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1880, opens behind an old farm-house. A girl named Ollie has been swinging in the grove for nearly an hour. Her mother calls her name from the house. Ollie stops the swing and hurries along the path. Mrs. Rogers stands at the back door holding a basket. She has been hunting for Ollie all over the house.

Sugar is what she needs, for new cookies. A recipe from Mrs. Coe uses more sugar than expected. The errand launches the story from a quiet domestic moment. No author is named on the pages shown. Readers meet a country household through a child's small, everyday duties.
the-young-firemen-of-lakeville-or-herber: Frank V. Webster's The Young Firemen of Lakeville, published in 1909, appears here through its front pages and opening contents. Webster's other boys' books are listed for young readers. Titles include Only a Farm Boy and Bob the Castaway. The contents begin with a midnight alarm. Peril follows, and Bert forms a plan. Herbert Dare's pluck is promised in the subtitle. The story chapters themselves start beyond the pages present in this record.
there-back: George MacDonald wrote the novel There and Back, and its contents list runs to forty chapters. Early headings introduce a father, child, and nurse, then a stepmother and a flight. Richard's story moves through a bookbinder, the Mansons, and Simon Armour. Later chapters centre on Barbara Wylder, Alice, Mortgrange, and the parson Wingfold, ending in London. MacDonald's Thomas Wingfold also appears by name in the headings. A contents list alone is shown in this record, so the novel's chapters themselves are not shown.
to-infidelity-and-back:
Evangelist Henry F. Lutz published his religious autobiography at Cincinnati in 1911, subtitled how he found Christ and his church. He dedicated it to pioneers of the nineteenth-century Restoration Movement, who endured poverty and persecution while seeking Christian union on the first, simple gospel. Their beacon light, he says, guided him.

An opening piece, written on his Bible's flyleaf after the struggle, describes emerging from a stormy sea of agony. Sectarianism, rationalism, infidelity, and doubt lacerated his soul. Readers get a truth-seeker's testimony meant for sensitive readers who have endured similar doubt and despair, framed by Isaiah and Bacon.
un-doc-letter-to-un-security-council-by-:
Sir Jeremy Greenstock, Britain's ambassador to the United Nations, sent this letter to the Security Council in 2003, during the crisis over Iraq. The letter put the British position into the Council's formal record. It belongs to the intense diplomacy that ran alongside the debate over war.

In the letter, Greenstock sets out Britain's reading of Iraq's duties under past Council resolutions. He explains why London saw Baghdad as still in breach of those duties. Historians value the letter as a primary record of the British case, stated in Britain's own words at the time.
